claims.statement: After Denmark's 2002 parental leave reform, employees of foundation-owned firms took 1.756 more weeks of parental leave than employees of family-owned firms (owner-managed or with a family majority on the board) (raw, unmatched sample of employees with a new child in foundation-owned and family-owned firms).

definition.value: Weeks of registered parental leave taken within 52 weeks of childbirth (barselsorlov under the Parental Leave Act), measured for employees with a new child; the dependent variable y_ijt in equation (1) is parental leave weeks for employee i in firm j at time t.

key_assumptions.assumption: Identification rests on the differential change in leave uptake between foundation firms and the comparison group (family-owned firms (owner-managed or with a family majority on the board)) after the 2002 reform rather than on strict parallel trends: absent the reform, the change in mean weeks of leave in foundation firms would have equalled the change in the comparison firms, conditional on the controls and fixed effects of equation (1).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states that its estimates rely on differential changes in matched firms rather than strict parallel trends, and reports that pre-trends tests (available on request) show foundation firms had lower pre-reform leave uptake, which it addresses by matching on observables; it concedes it cannot definitively rule out alternative explanations.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the employee controls (age, gender, education), firm controls (ln firm age, ln employees, ln total assets, leverage, export share, ROA), ROA × Post and industry and year fixed effects, and with no matching applied in this column, foundation ownership is unrelated to the counterfactual outcome.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The column includes the full control set and industry and year fixed effects (table notes); the paper applies no matching here and motivates matching elsewhere precisely because foundation and family firms differ on observables.

definition.value: Post_t in equation (1): an indicator for the post-reform period 2003-2004, capturing Denmark's 2002 parental leave reform, which extended job-protected, income-compensated leave from 26 to 52 weeks per birth and was implemented uniformly across all private-sector employers. β2 is the post-reform change in weeks of leave for the comparison (family-firm) group, i.e. at F_j = 0.

timing.value: Switches on in 2003-2004; pre-reform base period 2000-2001; the reform year 2002 is excluded from the sample.

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark matched employer-employee administrative data, 2000-2004 (the paper names no register code or register variable for the leave measure)

definition.value: Weeks of registered parental leave taken within 52 weeks of childbirth (barselsorlov under the Parental Leave Act), measured for employees with a new child; the dependent variable y_ijt in equation (1) is parental leave weeks for employee i in firm j at time t.

timing.value: Leave taken within 52 weeks of each childbirth, for births in 2000-2001 and 2003-2004 (reform year 2002 excluded); employees with several childbirths contribute several observations.

magnitude.interpretation: confirming that the reform substantially increased leave uptake across all firms

estimand.target_population: employees with a new child in the comparison group (family-owned firms), for whom β2 gives the post-reform change in weeks of leave
estimand.time_horizon: post-reform period 2003-2004 relative to the pre-reform base period 2000-2001 (reform year 2002 excluded)

population.description: employees with a new child, employed in foundation-owned firms or in this column's comparison group (family-owned firms), in Denmark, 2000-2004 excluding the reform year 2002; PSM-matched sample (caliper 0.01)
subgroups_defined: part-time vs full-time employees (Table 3 Panel B)
low tenure (< 2 years) vs high tenure (>= 2 years) (Table 3 Panel B)
alternative control groups: all private firms, family firms, foreign MNCs (Table 3 Panel A)
population.selection: employees with a new child linked to their employer in Statistics Denmark matched employer-employee data; foundation ownership from the Danish Business Authority's register; publicly listed corporations, cooperatives and state enterprises excluded from the main sample; propensity score matching (PSM) on the same pre-reform characteristics with a caliper of 0.01

identification.source_of_variation: Denmark's 2002 parental leave reform, which extended job-protected, income-compensated leave from 26 to 52 weeks per birth and applied uniformly to all private-sector employers, interacted with firm ownership form (foundation-owned vs family-owned firms); propensity score matching (PSM) on the same pre-reform characteristics with a caliper of 0.01

key_assumptions.assumption: The before-after change in weeks of leave in the comparison group, conditional on the controls and fixed effects of equation (1), is attributable to the 2002 reform: absent the reform, mean leave would not have changed between 2000-2001 and 2003-2004.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper reads the positive Post-reform coefficient as confirming that the reform substantially increased leave uptake across all firms, and notes that the reform applied uniformly to all private-sector employers; it offers no separate test of this before-after assumption.

key_assumptions.assumption: After propensity score matching with a caliper of 0.01 on the same pre-reform characteristics used for CEM, and conditional on the employee and firm controls, ROA × Post and industry and year fixed effects, foundation ownership is unrelated to the counterfactual outcome.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states that PSM with a caliper of 0.01 is implemented as robustness on the same pre-reform characteristics; no balance test or propensity-score distribution is reported.

Any differential response must therefore work through the firm, not the law.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Institutional background section: the policy was implemented uniformly across all private-sector employers, and the foundation's special legal status does not extend to the firms it owns.
